description: A team of young engineers, programmers, and innovators united by a passion for exploring space, working with open scientific data, and developing technological solutions for the future.
summary:
Field Shift is a web tool that helps US farmers explore crop rotations for one specific field. The farmer picks a field on a satellite map, sets what matters most (saving water, soil health, erosion, income), and the tool compares the current rotation with three alternatives: adding a cover crop, adding a legume or small grain, and swapping in a crop that needs less water. Each option gets a score from 0 to 100, a plain-language explanation, a planting calendar, the evidence behind it, and a list of things to check with a local agronomist.

The tool combines NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER climate, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI) with USDA soil, crop history and prices, and FAO crop water needs. It addresses the challenge by turning open data that farmers cannot easily read into a clear and honest comparison for their own field. This matters because rain and heat are changing, and a good rotation protects soil and water. Field Shift supports the farmer's judgment and does not replace local expertise.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Field Shift compares the crop rotation a field has now with three alternatives and explains each one in plain words. It works for any farm field in the 48 contiguous US states. The interface is in English and Ukrainian, and the report can be printed or saved as PDF.

HOW IT WORKS

1. The farmer clicks a field on the map (or searches a place) and sets priorities: water, soil health, erosion, income. They can also say if they have irrigation, livestock, or small-grain equipment.

2. NASA POWER gives 25 years (2001-2025) of daily weather for the point. We turn it into frost dates, growing degree days, season rainfall, heat days, heavy-rain days, and dry and wet years.

3. USDA SSURGO gives the soil: organic matter, slope, and how easily it erodes.

4. USDA Cropland Data Layer (2016-2025) shows what was grown each year, so the tool detects the current rotation by itself.

5. FAO GAEZ gives the water need and water shortage of each crop on this field, for today and for 2041-2070.

6. NASA satellites check the picture: GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP root-zone soil moisture, and MODIS NDVI, which shows how green the field was each season compared with other years of the same crop.

7. The tool builds three alternatives and scores all four options from 0 to 100 on six criteria: water use, soil health, erosion control, pest break, income, and weather resilience. The farmer's priorities set the weights. A switch shows a typical, dry, or wet year.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A farmer gets one clear suggestion in a minute or two instead of reading satellite files. They see when the field is bare, which years the crop was weaker, and which rotation fits their goals. We hope it helps farmers try rotations that keep soil covered, use less water, and stay profitable.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Every statement shows its source and a tag: measured or model. Each option lists what we do not know and what to check locally. If there is no farm field at the chosen point (a town, forest, or water), the tool explains why and does not invent data. Scores are simple, open rules, so a farmer can see why an option got its number.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Farmers may have little technical experience, so the first screen after analysis is one suggestion in plain words, with details one click away. Different data sources cover different years, so we use long periods for climate and recent years for the state of the field. Limits: some crop traits and the score formulas are our own simple estimates and were not checked by agronomists; the analysis is for one point, not for zones inside a field.

TOOLS

Backend: Python, FastAPI. Frontend: React, Vite, Leaflet, Recharts, Figma. Hosting: Render and Railway. Code: GitHub.
